accuracy.reason: All nine objectives are taught with accurate scope: embedded persistent SQL, affinity versus STRICT, explicit foreign-key verification, configured durability, one writer, same-host WAL, conditional index usefulness and consistent backup requirements. No false transaction, writer or recovery guarantee.

evidence.quote: Constrain references to existing rows; null references are allowed unless separately forbidden. Before starting a transaction, enable enforcement on each connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, then query PRAGMA foreign_keys and check that it returns 1.
WAL still allows only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine.

mechanisms.reason: The process/file diagram explains embedded access; journal versus WAL explains undo versus append/checkpoint and reader snapshots. Writer-slot contention, bounded waits and transaction retry explain failure behavior. The WAL and index diagrams preserve these mechanisms without asserting automatic parallel writers or forced plans.

evidence.quote: A connection can receive this result when it cannot obtain required access. A busy timeout or bounded retry can tolerate brief contention; some failures require retrying the transaction. Waiting does not create another writer or guarantee success.
Transfers logged changes into the main database file. Long-running reads can delay checkpoint progress and allow the log to grow.

coherence.reason: Local execution and workload fit lead to typing/rules and transactions, then concurrency and journaling, then query cost and operational responsibility. All card objectives inform the final locality/concurrency/recovery decision. The prerequisites are adequate for this explanation.

evidence.quote: The key questions are where the data lives and how much work competes to write it. SQLite is not limited to prototypes.

decisions.reason: Choice is tied to where access occurs, write contention and transaction duration, with a client/server alternative for shared sustained writes. The deck includes configuration, index maintenance, checkpoint growth, synchronization, migration and tested restore costs without arbitrary user-count limits.

evidence.quote: Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns. SQLite can still be suitable behind an application server with local storage.
Manage access permissions and free space. Retain backups according to recovery needs, then test restoration and application usability. A backup file alone does not prove consistency or recovery time.

clarity.reason: Embedded/serverless, affinity, STRICT, ACID, busy results, WAL/checkpoint, composite index and migration are directly defined. Short diagrams make process and storage boundaries visible. The busy-wait and backup qualifications prevent tempting but unsupported simplifications.

evidence.quote: The engine runs inside your application's process. Your code calls SQLite directly, rather than sending queries to a separate database server.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria are supported by slides 1–2, 5 and 8–9: in-process SQL, persistent relational transactions, remaining host responsibilities, local/service fit, shared-network workload limits and no universal user-count or synchronization guarantee. Learner addresses operational responsibility in its query/operations and final answers; evidence entails it.

All eight criteria explicitly taught by slides 3–4 and reconstructed correctly: flexible affinity/STRICT; primary/unique/not-null/check roles; per-connection foreign-key verification before transactions; declared rather than automatic rules; transaction atomicity/consistency; isolation limits; settings/storage durability; and external-side-effect exclusion.

All eight criteria supported by slides 4–6 and diagrams: multiple connections versus one writer, access contention and busy results, short transactions with bounded waits/transaction retry, no success guarantee, undo versus WAL mechanisms, stable readers with one writer, checkpoint obstruction/growth, and same-host locking/shared-memory limits.

All eight criteria supported by slides 7–8: index/plan definition, owner/time candidate and measurement, legitimate scans, local resource and maintenance costs, permissions/capacity, coordinated migrations, committed WAL state requiring a supported consistent backup, and tested usable recovery. The supported-backup branch satisfies the criterion; an unprovided quiescence procedure is not credited.

All four criteria satisfied by the actual learner using the full lesson: conditional single-host fit, shared sustained-write reasons for evaluating client/server, explicit rules/transactions/query measurement/backups, and measurements of contention/duration/busy behavior/locality/query and recovery needs. It labels unknown performance thresholds rather than inventing them.

sourceChecks.claim: Opened SQLite appropriate-uses documentation: local application/device storage and relational server comparison support embedded deployment fit. In-memory support is also demonstrated by the linked backup API documentation.
Appropriate-uses page checked for local, embedded and web application cases; workload/location/concurrent writes drive fit rather than prototype status.

Opened STRICT documentation including coercion and ANY. Constraint null rules checked at https://www.sqlite.org/lang_createtable.html; per-connection PRAGMA verification and no-op inside transactions at https://www.sqlite.org/foreignkeys.html.

Opened exact synchronous pragma anchor and inspected NORMAL/FULL/OFF failure differences. Isolation documentation supports visibility scope; WAL and backup sources support persistent-state boundaries. No claim that all commits survive every power/storage failure.

Opened isolation documentation, including SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT requiring rollback and a new transaction. Single-writer/multiple-connection behavior and non-guaranteed waiting are correctly represented.

Opened WAL documentation: original journal versus appended changes, snapshot end marks, checkpoint restriction by long reads, single writer and same-host shared memory are verified. WAL diagram shows committed data moving by checkpoint without promising all log content is committed.

Opened query-planner documentation and its multicolumn search/sort example. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN additionally checked at https://www.sqlite.org/eqp.html. Candidate index diagram is appropriately subject to measurement and planner choice.

Opened backup API documentation: completed supported backups yield consistent snapshots. WAL-file persistent-state warning checked at https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html; table rebuild/copy migration procedure at https://www.sqlite.org/lang_altertable.html. Recovery tests are correctly required beyond file existence.

Appropriate-uses page supports the local versus network-shared concurrency trade-off; WAL and isolation sources verify limitations. The card offers requirements-based guidance without asserting a universal workload threshold.
